title: A sudden change after a loose connection
summary: Recognise suspected air embolism, explain the immediate response and discuss safe review before further dialysis.

stages.narrative: In this fictional unit scenario, an adult on maintenance HD suddenly coughs, struggles to breathe and becomes confused. A nurse sees bubbles in the venous return tubing near a loosened connection. The patient was talking normally moments earlier.
prompts: Which findings make a dialysis-related emergency plausible?
Would a definitive diagnostic test be needed before protecting the patient?
teaching_points: The temporal change and visible air make air embolism a serious working diagnosis. Other causes of sudden deterioration still require assessment.

sources.locator: Section 2.2 Air Embolus, printed p2 / physical PDF p4: signs, causes and immediate management steps 1, 2, 5-7; positioning and aspiration steps 3-4 excluded

stages.narrative: Reveal: the team treats the presentation as suspected air embolism and activates the unit emergency response. A colleague proposes routine blood return to avoid losing the circuit volume.
prompts: What must happen to the pump and access while help arrives?
Why is routine blood return inappropriate here?
teaching_points: Stop the pump and clamp access and bloodlines; withhold circuit blood. Trained staff assess airway, breathing and circulation and provide oxygen support while emergency help attends.
This is a parallel emergency response, not an instruction to complete machine troubleshooting before attending to the patient.

stages.narrative: Debrief: after emergency transfer, the patient asks whether the machine alarm alone should have prevented the event. The unit reviews the connection, alarm history and circumstances with the patient before planning the next treatment.
prompts: What should the review establish before treatment resumes?
Which parts of a full emergency protocol have not been taught here?
teaching_points: Review the route of possible air entry and the response to alarms before deciding how dialysis can safely continue. A reset is not evidence that the cause has been corrected.
Positioning, air aspiration and hyperbaric referral need separate clinical and local-protocol assessment; this case does not teach or assess those procedures.

title: The blood looks different
summary: Connect an intradialytic symptom cluster to suspected haemolysis, potassium risk and investigation before re-exposure.

stages.narrative: A fictional adult develops chest tightness and nausea during HD. Staff notice unusually cherry-red, translucent blood beyond the dialyser. Blood pressure is initially raised. There is no external bleeding.
prompts: Which hazard links the symptoms and blood appearance?
Does the raised pressure rule it out?
teaching_points: Suspect haemolysis and assess urgently; hypotension is not a required early feature. The appearance is a warning sign, not a stand-alone confirmatory test.

sources.locator: Section 2.10 Hemolysis, printed pp8-9 / physical PDF pp10-11: definition, signs, immediate management, bloodwork/ECG and equipment investigation

stages.narrative: Reveal: the team stops dialysis and clamps the venous line. One trainee asks whether the circuit blood should be returned before blood tests are taken.
prompts: Which immediate physiological complication needs assessment?
teaching_points: Do not return suspected haemolysed circuit blood. Red-cell disruption releases potassium, so urgent potassium assessment and ECG monitoring matter alongside haemolysis investigations.

stages.narrative: Debrief: another patient in the same unit develops a similar symptom pattern. The clinical lead coordinates urgent assessment, and biomedical staff retain the affected equipment for investigation. No cause has yet been confirmed.
prompts: How does the second event change the investigation?
What would be wrong with simply restarting the original circuit after the symptoms improve?
teaching_points: A cluster warrants investigation of a shared exposure, including dialysate, as well as tubing or equipment problems. It does not prove a particular contaminant.
Further dialysis requires a safe treatment arrangement after clinical and technical review. Retain implicated equipment for investigation; symptom improvement alone does not clear it for reuse.

title: Wetness without an alarm
summary: Recognise disconnection bleeding, distinguish access-specific first actions and understand the contaminated-circuit boundary.

stages.narrative: In a fictional dialysis session, a patient tells staff that the sleeve over the fistula suddenly feels wet. The machine has not alarmed. On immediate inspection the venous needle is displaced and blood is escaping.
prompts: How much reassurance does the silent alarm provide?
teaching_points: A silent pressure alarm cannot exclude dislodgement. Stop the pump, summon help and apply pressure to the fistula bleeding site while assessing the patient.

Physical PDF pp4-5: Observation, Pressure Monitoring, and Principles of Safe Alarm Handling (MARC); review date April 2026 on physical p5

stages.narrative: Reveal: the exposed circuit end has touched the floor. Bleeding is being controlled. During handover, staff also discuss how a separated catheter connection would differ from this fistula needle event.
prompts: Should blood from the contaminated circuit be returned?
What access-specific protective action is described for a catheter?
teaching_points: Withhold blood from the contaminated circuit. Continue urgent assessment of blood loss; this does not establish a universal discard rule for every bleed.
For a catheter disconnection, trained staff secure the access by clamping; for the bleeding fistula needle site, pressure controls the external loss.

sources.locator: Section 2.16.1 VA Disconnection/Needle Dislodgement (Arterial or Venous), printed p15 / physical PDF p17: signs, management and prevention; excludes section 2.16.2 rupture

stages.narrative: Debrief: the patient explains that they covered the arm because they felt cold. The team discusses comfort, visibility and how to report wetness, then reviews securement and observation arrangements before the next session.
prompts: How can the patient participate in a safer next-session plan?
Why must staff assess the patient and connections before resetting a pressure alarm?
teaching_points: Agree how to keep the access visible while addressing comfort, and encourage prompt reporting of wetness or bleeding. Alarms supplement direct observation.
Assess the patient, connections and alarm cause; correct the problem before reset and confirm that treatment can continue safely.
